entry.title: How to Use Siri & Visual Intelligence on Anything in MacOS 27 with a Keystroke
entry.content:
Visual Intelligence offers a set of AI features that can be used to identify objects and items in photos or things on screen, and a neat new feature available in MacOS 27 Golden Gate allows you to interact with Siri and Visual Intelligence from just about anywhere on your Mac. You can use this to help identify things in pictures, understand a document, or even to learn what a particular file or app is for if you aren’t sure.

This this feature is available in MacOS 27 or later, meaning it obviously requires MacOS 27 Golden Gate or newer to have access to this particular Siri + Visual Intelligence feature.

How to Use Visual Intelligence & Ask Siri for Any Item on Mac Screen

This trick is two parts and remarkably simple; have the item or image you are curious about as your active window on the Mac, then hit the appropriate keyboard shortcut to access Visual Intelligence to query about the active window:

  • Shift + Command + Spacebar to open Ask Siri AI with Visual Intelligence for the active window, then type your query and hit return

This brings up a little “Ask Siri” query that you can then type your question or request into:

For example, if you have a photo of a plant open on your Mac, hit Shift+Command+Spacebar, then type something like “what type of plant is this”, and Siri and Visual Intelligence will report back to describe and label the plant.

Or, as the screenshot examples here show, you can also have something visible on screen, and then hit Command+Shift+Spacebar and simply ask “describe this” and Siri AI Visual Intelligence will then identify and describe what the image is of.

In the photo examples here, you’ll see it’s a picture of an Apple II that Siri AI and Visual Intelligence accurately recognizes and then provides information about.

Another example that is quite handy; have Finder open to a random file, app, or system component that you are unsure? Hit Command+Shift+Spacebar and ask “what is this”. In the screenshot example here, we are using this tool to accurately identify a system daemon found within a system folder of MacOS.

This has many uses, and is really quite useful. In every test example I gave Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, it was able to accurately describe what it was provided, and to give useful and accurate information about various files, photos, webpages, and other items.

This “Ask Siri” keyboard shortcut can be accessed anywhere on the Mac, and generally behaves similar to the Write with Siri floating button that appears in text-entry boxes in the latest MacOS versions.

For what it’s worth, you can also use the “Ask ChatGPT” feature of Spotlight to perform similar functionality, if you provide it with an image.

Give this feature a try, you might be surprised at how capable it is, and how useful it can be!

entry.title: Fix dasd Using 100% CPU on MacOS 27
entry.content:
I ran into a peculiar issue recently where the ‘dasd’ process had been consuming 100% CPU for several days straight. Since dasd is a system process, my initial assumption was that there must be some important background task that was going on. But, after a few days of no change and dasd constantly hovering between 90-100% CPU usage, contributing to significant battery drain and resource misallocation, I decided to dive into troubleshooting dasd consuming large amount of processor specifically in MacOS 27 Golden Gate.

With the help of some tinkering around in Console and Terminal, an agent, and ChatGPT, I discovered the problem with dasd going haywire may be related to an issue with telemetry and the PowerLog background processing database in MacOS. And, as it turns out, clearing this particular database and then restarting the Mac can resolve the problem.

Be forewarned, these steps involve using the Terminal to delete a system file that is actively being written to, so something could always go wrong. Backup your Mac before beginning.

Troubleshooting dasd with all the traditional methods, to no end

First, I tried killing the ‘dasd’ process with Activity Monitor, which did nothing. I rebooted, that did nothing either, and dasd persisted with 100% CPU usage even after restart, unusual! Next I rebooted into Safe Mode, which also did nothing as the ‘dasd’ process continued to use excessive CPU even in Safe Mode. So I rebooted again, and after digging around in diagnostics and going back and forth between Console, sample, and tail, and ChatGPT to interpret and analyze, I arrived at this solution.

Identifying a database linked to stuck dasd

The database in question that dasd appears to be interacting with in some erroneous looping and stuck manner is located at the following system path:

/private/var/db/powerlog/Library/PerfPowerTelemetry/BackgroundProcessing/CurrentBackgroundProcessingDB.BGSQL

I backed up and erased this particular database, then restarted the Mac, and that finally resolved the problem, bringing dasd back down to 0% CPU as expected.

Backup your Mac, and the database file itself

If you have and use Time Machine for backups of your Mac, that’s probably sufficient, and you should absolutely make a Time Machine backup before continuing. Separately, if you’re like me and want to make a direct separate file backup as well (just in case!) on the same drive, here’s how you can do that.

From Terminal, and copy / paste or type the following command string to create a Folder on your desktop called “PowerLog-Backup” that contains a backup of the PowerLog database with permissions assigned to the current user:
sudo mkdir -p ~/Desktop/PowerLog-Backup | sudo cp -p /private/var/db/powerlog/Library/PerfPowerTelemetry/BackgroundProcessing/CurrentBackgroundProcessingDB.BGSQL* ~/Desktop/PowerLog-Backup/ | sudo chown -R "$(id -un)" ~/Desktop/PowerLog-Backup

If you’d rather break that into three separate commands you can do that with:

sudo mkdir -p ~/Desktop/PowerLog-Backup

sudo cp -p /private/var/db/powerlog/Library/PerfPowerTelemetry/BackgroundProcessing/CurrentBackgroundProcessingDB.BGSQL* ~/Desktop/PowerLog-Backup/

sudo chown -R "$(id -un)" ~/Desktop/PowerLog-Backup

Carefully Delete the PowerLog Database

Now it is time to reset the PowerLog database. This involves deleting a system file so if you are not comfortable with that, or if you do not have a full backup of your data, do not use this command. The command must be entered precisely to avoid accidentally deleting the wrong system file which could result in a bigger problem:

sudo rm \
/private/var/db/powerlog/Library/PerfPowerTelemetry/BackgroundProcessing/CurrentBackgroundProcessingDB.BGSQL \
/private/var/db/powerlog/Library/PerfPowerTelemetry/BackgroundProcessing/CurrentBackgroundProcessingDB.BGSQL-wal \
/private/var/db/powerlog/Library/PerfPowerTelemetry/BackgroundProcessing/CurrentBackgroundProcessingDB.BGSQL-shm

Execute that command with root priveleges.

Restart the Mac right away, wait a few minutes and check CPU again

Then restart the Mac immediately, which you can initiate from the  Apple menu or from Terminal with:

sudo reboot

After your Mac restarts, check CPU usage after the reboot settles, and again in 10 minutes or so. Now, if you review Activity Monitor, or returning to the command line with:

ps -axo pid,%cpu,etime,command | grep '[d]asd'

You should now find that CPU usage for dasd is back down to 0% or some minimal inconsequential amount.

–

The above steps are what worked for resolving high constant CPU usage of dasd for my Mac running MacOS 27.0.1, after the dasd process had been using 90% to 100% CPU for several days straight.

Not common, but problems with dasd and excess CPU and memory usage are not nonexistent

How prevalent this issue is, is not known, since it may be impacting more Mac users but they’re not actively finding the ‘dasd’ process in Activity Monitor, or don’t know to even look, despite battery draining a bit faster than normal, or their Mac feeling warm to the touch. The cause is also unknown.

If you happen to search around the web for this issue, you might discover that other Mac users around the web have complained of issues with dasd recently in MacOS 27 as well, so this could be a bug that will get ironed out in a future software update for MacOS.

Those discussions were on Reddit, MacRumors Forums (2), and Apple discussion boards. You’ll also find some solutions that were not effective for me, some focused on constantly killing the process, or unloading it with launchctl, the App Store, or Apple Arcade, none of which were related to dasd going haywire with CPU usage in my particular case.

There are other variations of this issue with ‘dasd’ and some users find the dasd process does not hog 100% CPU but instead dasd may consume hugely inordinate amounts of RAM, or that dasd is generating enormous log files.

It’s not entirely clear what is causing the issue with dasd, and while trial and error and troubleshooting led me to the PowerLog telemetry database, that could simply be downstream of something else. If you run into this problem with dasd (or a similar one), and find another solution, or use the solution here and it works, share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: MacOS Golden Gate 27.2 Update Available to Download
entry.content:
Apple has released MacOS 27.2 Golden Gate, the update includes new Siri AI features and support for Siri AI in additional languages, along with miscellaneous nonspecific bug fixes and security patches. Release notes are included below, along with download links for the full installer and IPSW file for MacOS 27.2.

Separately, Apple has also released MacOS Tahoe 26.7.2, MacOS Sequoia 15.8.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, along with 27.2 updates for WatchOS, tvOS, HomePod OS with SoundGlow support, and more, so check for updates on your other Apple devices as well.

And for those who are confused by versioning and numbers, apparently MacOS 27.2 leapfrogged MacOS 27.1 which was never released to the public, and the same applies to iOS 27.2 which leapfrogged iOS 27.1 that was also never released.

How to Download & Install MacOS 27.2 Golden Gate Update

Be sure to backup Mac with Time Machine or your method of choice before installing a system software update.

  1. From the  Apple menu, go to “System Settings”
  2. Go to “General” and then choose “Software Update”
  3. Choose to “Update Now” for MacOS 27.2 in software update

MacOS 27.2 will then download and install, rebooting the Mac to complete installation.

The download is over 14GB in size, and a reminder that installing MacOS updates can take a while to finish, so do not interrupt the process.

Mac users who are not running MacOS 27 will find an update to MacOS Tahoe or MacOS Sequoia available instead.

MacOS 27.2 Full Installer & IPSW Direct Download Links

Downloading the full installer or an IPSW file for MacOS 27.2 is easy through Apple CDN server links below:

MacOS Tahoe 26.7.2 & MacOS Sequoia 15.8.2 Full Installer Download Links

We maintain an updated list of all available MacOS installers and IPSW files as well.

MacOS 27.2 Golden Gate Release Notes

Release notes mentioned new Siri AI features but are otherwise short and not particularly detailed in terms of what bugs are fixed or other changes are included:

This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context. It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation. This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

Don’t forget to update all of your other Apple devices as well, since Apple has released software updates to many other devices too.

entry.title: iOS 27.2 Update for iPhone & iPad Released
entry.content:
Apple has released iOS 27.2 for iPhone, and ipadOS 27.2 for iPad. These updates include new Siri AI features, along with Siri AI support in new languages, unspecified bug fixes, and security patches, making them recommended for all iPhone and iPad users to install.

Additionally, Apple has also released MacOS 27.2 for Golden Gate users, MacOS Tahoe 26.7.2 update, HomePod OS 27.2 with support for Sound Glow on HomePod Mini and HomePod second gen, iOS 26.7.2, iPadOS 26.7.2, iOS 18.7.11, and iPadOS 18.7.11, tvOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, and more, so you will want to update all of your Apple devices.

How to Download & Install iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 Update

Always backup iPhone or iPad to iCloud before beginning system software updates.

  1. Open the “Settings” app on your iPhone or iPad
  2. Go to “General” and then go to “Software Update”
  3. Choose to “Update Now” for iOS 27.2 or iPadOS 27.2

The iPhone or iPad will download, restart, and install the update.

Users can also choose to update manually, or with IPSW files.

iOS 27.2 Update Release Notes

Release notes included with the iOS 27.2 update download are as follows:

iOS 27.2

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15
Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)
– Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week
– Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List
– Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting
– Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need
– Siri AI is available in more languages, with support tor French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Siri AI is not available in the EU or mainland China

Other
– Suggestions in Messages help you take action based on the context of your conversations, like adding a Calendar invite for a dinner
– Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos
– Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground
– The Home tab in the Podcasts app offers two separate sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing, letting you find the latest updates from your shows and then pick up where you left off
– Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages
– Simple Profiles in the Apple TV app lets everyone in your household have their own profile, with recommendations that fit what they like to watch
– FaceTime supports adding a third party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call

iOS 27.2 IPSW Firmware Download Links

The links below point iOS 27.2 IPSW on Apple CDN servers:

iPadOS 27.2 IPSW

Don’t forget to update your other Apple devices as well, most of which also received software updates today.

Wait, iOS 27.2? What happened to iOS 27.1?

As far as versioning and numerical releases go, you may have noticed this is iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2, along with MacOS 27.2 and other OS 27.2 updates… and yes that means iOS 27.1, iPadOS 27.1, MacOS 27.1, and all OS 27.1 releases, were skipped by Apple. Why that is the case is not clear, but if you are confused by missing that interim update, don’t be, OS 27.2 is where we are all at with these updates.

Separately, Apple has also released MacOS 27.2 Golden Gate, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, iOS 26.7.2, iPadOS 26.7.2, iOS 18.7.11, iPadOS 18.7.11, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, along with updates to just about every other Apple device, so you’ll want to check for and install updates elsewhere too.

entry.title: Apple Updates MacBook Pro & iMac to M6 Chip, iPad Mini with 8.5″ OLED Display
entry.content:
Apple has released a series of hardware updates this week, including an updated iPad Mini with A20 chip and OLED display, an iMac with M6 chip, and a 14″ MacBook Pro base model with M6 chip. These products were announced ahead of the “Pro and Tell” event set for tomorrow, which is expected to launch a touchscreen MacBook Pro.

14″ MacBook Pro with M6 Chip

The base-model MacBook Pro 14″ now includes an M6 chip with 12-core CPU and GPU, better AI performance, and improved memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7 support, and is available in the same color options as before. Notably, the new base model MacBook Pro comes with a 1TB SSD, along with 16GB RAM.

Pricing begins at $1999, with pre-orders on October 28.

iMac with M6 Chip

Apple has updated the 24″ iMac lineup to include the new powerful M6 chip, which boosts performance considerably with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, and improved AI performance. The iMac M6 comes standard with 16GB RAM and a 256GB storage, and is available in the same set of color options as prior models, including green, blue, purple, yellow, orange, red, and silver.

Pricing starts at $1499, with pre-orders starting October 28 and availability on November 6.

iPad Mini with A20 Chip and OLED Display

The iPad Mini has now been updated to include an A20 Pro chip, and the LCD screen has been replaced with a slightly larger 8.5″ OLED display which allows for darker blacks but comes at the cost of PWM which impacts some users eyes (yours truly included). The device also includes a 12MP center stage front-facing camera, wi-fi 7 support, Apple Pencil support, water and dust resistance, and is available in space grey and silverlight colors.

Pricing for iPad Mini now starts at $699 for wi-fi models, and $849 for cellular equipped models. Pre-orders start October 28 for November 6 delivery.

–

Not yet launched, but expected to arrive tomorrow, is the all-new touchscreen MacBook Pro. Stay tuned for more details on that, as the announcement is made.

That all covers the hardware side of things, but don’t forget the software side, where Apple has released a whole bevy of system software updates for nearly every Apple device, including iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, HomePod OS 27.2 with support for Sound Glow, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, iOS 26.7.2, MacOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and several hundred security patches are included in both MacOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and MacOS Tahoe 26.7.2 (and yes the same security patches are included the other software updates too).

entry.title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro Launched by Apple
entry.content:
Apple has launched two all-new touchscreen MacBook Pro models, with 14″ and 16″ OLED display sizes. This marks a notable reversal from Apple against their longstanding resistance to touch screen laptops due to ergonomic issues.

The new MacBook Pro features a redesigned enclosure, M5 Pro or M5 Max chip options with up to 128GB RAM and 16GB of storage, a smaller Dynamic Island cutout replaces The Notch on the display, and is lighter weight than predecessors, weighing 3lbs for the 14″ model, and 4lbs for the 16″ model. A notable welcome return is the reintroduction of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the MacBook Pro.


There is full gesture support for the touchscreen, allowing for gestures like pinch to zoom, scrolling, and swiping between pages, slides, or Spaces. Apple Pencil is not supported.

The touchscreen MacBook Pro includes a front-facing FaceTime camera, three Thunderbolt 5 / USB-C ports, HDMI port, SDXC card slot, MagSafe for power, and a headphone jack.

The touchscreen display itself is OLED, and available in both 14″ and 16″ sizes, which Apple is calling the PROLED XDR Display. Presumably the display will have perceptible PWM like most OLED and LED-adjacent screens have, which could dissuade some PWM sensitive users from being able to use the Mac.

The 14″ touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2899, while the 16″ touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $3399. Pre-orders are live now and the touchscreen MacBook Pro will be available on November 6.

The video embedded below from X shows someone using the touch screen display to interact with MacOS:

And another:

And another:

As noted earlier, the introduction of a touchscreen Mac marks a departure from Apple’s prior stance on the matter. Apple had long been skeptical of touchscreen laptops, with Steve Jobs famously lamenting on the ergonomics of such a device (videos embedded are via X, you can find us there too):

The standard non-touch models of MacBook Pro are still available as well, the base model of which was just spec-bumped to the M6 chip.

The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the fourth major Apple product released this week, adding alongside to the A20 iPad Mini, M6 MacBook Pro, and M6 iMac.

entry.title: How to Boot in Safe Mode on MacBook Air, Neo, & Pro (Apple Silicon)
entry.content:
You may find yourself in a situation when you need to boot into Safe Mode while troubleshooting a MacBook Air, MacBook Neo, or MacBook Pro.

Safe Mode boots a Mac without loading third party login items, system extensions, and non-system fonts. Additionally, Safe Mode runs a disk check to verify the startup disk, clears system caches, and prevents third party drivers from loading, helping to narrow down potential issues, and sometimes even resolve them through the safe mode boot itself.

If you’re unfamiliar with booting into Safe Mode on modern Apple Silicon equipped MacBook laptops, including the Air, Neo, and Pro, it’s a pretty easy process that is the same on all Apple Silicon Macs, including M1, M2, M3, M4, M5, M6, A18 chips.

How to Boot in Safe Mode on MacBook Air, Pro, Neo

  1. If the Mac is currently turned on, you need to turn it off by going go the  Apple menu and selecting “Shut Down”
  2. When the Mac is off, now press and hold the Power button / Touch ID button, and continue holding the Power/Touch ID button until you see “Loading startup options”
  3. At the startup disk screen, now hold down the SHIFT key and click on “Continue in Safe Mode” and select “Macintosh HD” (or your boot disk)

  4. Once Safe Mode has started booting, you can release Shift key

The Mac will now be in Safe Mode, where you can perform whatever troubleshooting tasks you had in mind.

As mentioned before, simply booting into Safe Mode can sometimes remedy an issue if it’s related to a cache or third party extension or tool. If the problem is absent in Safe Mode but you boot normally again and the problem returns, that suggests the issue is related to some third party extension, tool, login item, or otherwise.

And sometimes problems persist in Safe Mode too, which usually suggests a system level problem. I ran into that recently when troubleshooting ‘dasd’ process 100% CPU usage over several days, even in safe mode, and eventually resolved that issue by removing a corrupt system database.

Exiting Safe Mode and Booting Normally Again

  1. Simply restart the Mac as usual to boot the Mac as normal, from the  Apple menu choose “Restart”

This process obviously covers Apple Silicon Mac laptops with Touch ID and the power button, but if you have an older Intel Mac you can use Safe Mode on those Macs too by simply holding Shift key during the entire boot process, arguably a bit easier.

entry.title: How to Enable Sound Glow on HomePod & HomePod Mini
entry.content:
Sound Glow is a snazzy new feature introduced for HomePod (2nd gen and later), and HomePod Mini (1st gen and later) that allows the small display on the top of the smart speaker to show a fun little ambient light effect that reacts to the rhythm, beat, and color of whatever you are playing on the device. It adds a bit of character to the HomePod that is particularly enjoyable in a dimmer or dark room. Curiously, Sound Glow is not enabled by default, so if you wish to use the feature you will have to turn it on manually, which we will show you how to do here.

Sound Glow System Requirements

Sound Glow is compatible with HomePod (2nd gen and later), and HomePod Mini (1st gen and later). The first gen HomePod does not support the feature.

Additionally, Sound Glow requires you to update your HomePod to HomeOS 27.2 (or whatever they’re calling it). That’ll happen automatically if you have a paired iPhone or iPad with iOS 27.2, or a Mac with MacOS 27.2. If your HomePod is not yet updated, you can do that manually from a Mac or iPhone/iPad within the Home app.

You will also want to update Spotify, Podcasts, and other apps, so they can support the feature fully.

How to Enable Sound Glow on HomePod & HomePod Mini

Assuming you meet the requirements and have your devices updated, here’s how to enable Sound Glow, which curiously is not enabled by default:

  1. Open the “Home” app on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac running iOS 27.2 or MacOS 27.2
  2. Long-press or right-click on the HomePod and choose “Accessory Settings”

  3. Scroll down and look for the “Sound Glow” option and toggle it ON

  4. Exit out of Home app
  5. Now open Music.app, Spotify, Podcasts, or another similar compatible app, and play audio through the HomePod to see SoundGlow in action

You should see the colors start to move and change on the little display atop HomePod right away, which will vary depending on the music and beat or what you are listening to.

The Sound Glow setting describes the feature as “Display ambient light that responds to the colors and rhythm of what’s playing.”

Note that some music and audio streams seem to be a little slower to adapt or catch onto Sound Glow, particularly through third party apps, so if you aren’t seeing immediate feedback you might try Music app or Podcasts app, and you’ll want to be sure to update Spotify and other apps to their latest versions just in case too.

If you have a HomePod, try it out yourself, it’s a fun new feature and worth enabling on your Apple smart speakers.

This is obviously for compatible HomePod devices, and it remains to be seen if HomeView will have a similar Sound Glow feature, perhaps on the screen itself, but we will find that out soon.
